titleStmt.title: Shiji 史记 · 秦庄襄王三年

bibl.title: 无骨者伊瓦尔《战国历史地图·年表》

div.head: Shiji I: Basic Annals
div.p: Basic Annals of Qin: In the third year Meng Ao attacked Wei's Gaodu and Ji and took them. He attacked Zhao's Yuci, Xincheng and Langmeng and took thirty-seven Fortresses. In April there was an eclipse of the sun. Wang He attacked Shangdang. Taiyuan Commandery was established for the first time. The Wei general Wuji led the troops of five states against Qin, and Qin fell back to Hewai. Meng Ao was defeated, broke off and withdrew. In May, on the day Bingwu, King Zhuangxiang died, and his son Zheng was set up: this was the First Emperor of Qin.

div.head: Shiji II: Tables
div.p: Qin: Wang Yi struck Shangdang. Taiyuan Commandery was established for the first time.
Prince Wuji of Wei led five states and drove our army back at Hewai; Meng Ao broke off and withdrew.
Wei: Wuji led the troops of five states and defeated the Qin army at Hewai.
Han: Qin took our Shangdang.

div.head: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
div.p: Hereditary House of Chu: In the sixteenth year, King Zhuangxiang of Qin died, and the King of Qin, Zhao Zheng, was set up.
Hereditary House of Zhao: In the nineteenth year, Zhao and Yan exchanged land: Zhao gave Longdui, Fenmen and Linle to Yan, and Yan gave Ge, Wuyang and Pingshu to Zhao.

Hereditary House of Wei: In the thirtieth year, Wuji returned to Wei, led the troops of five states to attack Qin, defeated them at Hewai and put Meng Ao to flight. The Heir Apparent of Wei, Zeng, was a hostage in Qin; Qin was angered and wished to imprison the Heir Apparent of Wei, Zeng. Someone said to the King of Qin on Zeng's behalf: "Gongsun Xi firmly told the Chancellor of Wei: 'Let Wei attack Qin hard; the King of Qin will be angered and will surely imprison Zeng. The King of Wei will be angered in turn and attack Qin, and Qin will surely be hurt.' Now if the King imprisons Zeng, Xi's plan has hit its mark. So it is better to honour Zeng and ally with Wei, so as to make Qi and Han suspicious of it." Qin thereupon let Zeng be.
Hereditary House of Han: In the twenty-sixth year, Qin took all our Shangdang.

div.head: Shiji IV: Biographies
div.p: Biography of the Prince of Wei: The King of Wei was angry that the Prince had stolen his army tally and killed Jin Bi under a feigned command, and the Prince knew it himself. Having driven back Qin and preserved Zhao, he had a general lead his army back to Wei, while the Prince alone stayed in Zhao with his retainers. King Xiaocheng of Zhao, grateful to the Prince for seizing Jin Bi's army under a feigned command and preserving Zhao, planned with Lord Pingyuan to enfeoff the Prince with five Fortresses. When the Prince heard of it, his mind grew proud and he wore the look of one who takes credit for his deed. One of his retainers said to the Prince: "There are things that must not be forgotten, and things that must not be remembered. When another has done the Prince a kindness, the Prince must not forget it; when the Prince has done another a kindness, I would have the Prince forget it. Moreover, to feign the King of Wei's command and seize Jin Bi's army to relieve Zhao was a service to Zhao, but towards Wei it was not the act of a loyal subject. For the Prince to grow proud and take credit for it — I privately think the Prince should not." At this the Prince at once reproached himself, as if there were nowhere he could hide. The King of Zhao swept the way and came to meet him in person, performed the rites of a host, and led the Prince towards the western steps. The Prince stepped aside in refusal and went up by the eastern steps. He declared his own fault: he had failed Wei and done no service to Zhao. The King of Zhao kept him at wine until dusk, and could not bring himself to offer the five Fortresses, because of the Prince's self-abasement. In the end the Prince stayed in Zhao. The King of Zhao gave the Prince Hao as his private estate, and Wei too restored Xinling for the Prince's support. The Prince remained in Zhao.

The Prince heard that in Zhao there were gentlemen in retirement: Master Mao, hidden among the gamblers, and Master Xue, hidden in the house of a seller of drinks. The Prince wished to see the two men, but the two hid themselves and would not see the Prince. When the Prince learned where they were, he went secretly on foot to keep company with the two, and they were very happy together. When Lord Pingyuan heard of it, he said to his wife: "At first I heard that your brother the Prince had no equal under Heaven; now I hear that he recklessly keeps company with gamblers and sellers of drinks — the Prince is a reckless man, that is all." His wife told the Prince. The Prince then took leave of his sister to go, saying: "At first I heard that Lord Pingyuan was a man of worth, and so I betrayed the King of Wei to relieve Zhao, to answer Lord Pingyuan's expectations. But Lord Pingyuan's company is only a grand display; he does not seek gentlemen. When Wuji was still in Daliang he often heard that these two were worthy men, and on coming to Zhao he feared he would not get to see them. With Wuji keeping their company, I still feared they would not want me; now Lord Pingyuan thinks it a disgrace — he is not worth keeping company with." And he packed to leave. His wife told Lord Pingyuan everything. Lord Pingyuan then took off his cap, apologised, and insisted that the Prince stay. When Lord Pingyuan's household heard of it, half of them left Lord Pingyuan and went over to the Prince, and the gentlemen of all under Heaven went over to the Prince once more; the Prince drew away Lord Pingyuan's retainers.

The Prince stayed in Zhao ten years without returning. Qin, hearing that the Prince was in Zhao, sent troops east day and night to attack Wei. The King of Wei was troubled by this and sent envoys to ask the Prince back. The Prince, fearing that the King was angry with him, warned his household: "Whoever dares to carry word for the King of Wei's envoys dies." His guests had all turned their backs on Wei for Zhao, and none dared urge the Prince to return. The two men Master Mao and Master Xue went to see the Prince and said: "The reason the Prince weighs heavily in Zhao and his name is heard among the Lords is solely that there is a Wei. Now Qin attacks Wei; Wei is in extremity and the Prince does not care. Should Qin destroy Daliang and level the ancestral temple of the former kings, with what face could the Prince stand before all under Heaven?" Before they had finished speaking the Prince's colour changed at once; he called for his carriage and hurried home to relieve Wei.

The King of Wei saw the Prince, and they wept together; and he gave the seal of Supreme General to the Prince, and the Prince took command. In the thirtieth year of King Anxi of Wei the Prince sent envoys to inform all the Lords. When the Lords heard that the Prince was in command, each sent generals with troops to relieve Wei. The Prince led the troops of five states and defeated the Qin army at Hewai, putting Meng Ao to flight. Then, following up the victory, he pursued the Qin army to Hangu Pass and held the Qin troops in check, so that the Qin troops dared not come out. At this time the Prince's majesty shook all under Heaven, and the retainers of the Lords presented methods of war, to all of which the Prince gave his name; hence the world at large calls them the Prince of Wei's Methods of War.

The King of Qin was troubled by this, and sent ten thousand jin of gold into Wei to seek out Jin Bi's former retainers and have them slander the Prince to the King of Wei: "The Prince was ten years in exile abroad; now he is Wei's general, and the generals of the Lords are all under him; the Lords hear only of the Prince of Wei and not of the King of Wei. The Prince also wishes to seize this moment to face south and make himself king; the Lords, in awe of the Prince's majesty, are about to set him up together." Qin several times sent agents of discord, feigning to congratulate the Prince on whether he had yet been set up as King of Wei. The King of Wei heard the slander daily and could not help believing it, and afterwards did indeed send someone to replace the Prince in command. The Prince, knowing that he had a second time been cast aside through slander, pleaded illness and did not attend court; with his guests he drank the night through, drinking strong wine and keeping much company with women. Day and night he made merry with drink for four years, and in the end died of drink. That same year King Anxi of Wei also died.

When Qin heard that the Prince was dead, it sent Meng Ao to attack Wei; he took twenty Fortresses, and Dong Commandery was first established. Thereafter Qin ate away at Wei little by little, as a silkworm eats a leaf, and in eighteen years it captured the King of Wei and slaughtered Daliang.

When Gaozu was still young and humble, he often heard of the Prince's worth. After he ascended the throne as Son of Heaven, whenever he passed Daliang he always sacrificed to the Prince. In the twelfth year of Gaozu, returning from the attack on Qing Bu, he established five tomb-keeping households for the Prince, to sacrifice to the Prince at the four seasons every year, generation after generation.

The Grand Historian says: I passed the ruins of Daliang and sought out what is called the Yi Gate. The Yi Gate was the eastern gate of the Fortress. Among the princes of all under Heaven there have been others who delighted in gentlemen, but that Lord Xinling received recluses of the caves and cliffs, and was not ashamed to associate with those beneath him, had its reason. That his name stood first among the Lords was no empty thing. And Gaozu, whenever he passed, had the people sacrifice to him without cease.

div.head: Shiji V: Biographies
div.p: Biography of Lü Buwei: King Zhuangxiang died in the third year after his accession; the Heir Apparent, Zheng, was set up as king, and he honoured Lü Buwei as Chancellor of State, styling him "Second Father". The King of Qin was young, and the Queen Dowager from time to time had secret relations with Lü Buwei. Buwei's household slaves numbered ten thousand.

At this time Wei had Lord Xinling, Chu had Lord Chunshen, Zhao had Lord Pingyuan and Qi had Lord Mengchang, all of whom humbled themselves before gentlemen and delighted in retainers, each striving to outdo the others. Lü Buwei, for all Qin's strength, was ashamed to fall short of them, and he too drew gentlemen to him and treated them generously, until his retainers reached three thousand. At that time there were many disputants among the Lords, such as Xun Qing and his kind, who wrote books and spread them over all under Heaven. Lü Buwei therefore had each of his guests write down what he had heard, and gathered their discourses into the Eight Surveys, Six Discourses and Twelve Records, more than two hundred thousand words. Holding that it comprised the affairs of heaven and earth, of the myriad things and of ancient and modern times, he called it Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals. He displayed it at the market gate of Xianyang, hung a thousand jin of gold above it, and invited the travelling gentlemen and retainers of the Lords: whoever could add or take away a single character would be given the thousand jin.

As the First Emperor grew to manhood, the Queen Dowager's licence did not cease. Lü Buwei, fearing that it would be found out and disaster fall on himself, privately sought out a man of great member, Lao Ai, and made him a household retainer; at times, letting the players and musicians loose, he had Ai walk with a wheel of tong wood hung on his member, and let the Queen Dowager hear of it, so as to bait her. The Queen Dowager heard, and as expected wished to have him in secret. Lü Buwei then presented Lao Ai, and had someone falsely accuse him of an offence meriting castration. Buwei also said to the Queen Dowager in private: "If the castration can be feigned, he can be had as a palace attendant." The Queen Dowager then secretly made rich gifts to the officer in charge of castrations, who passed false sentence on him, plucked out his beard and eyebrows and made him a eunuch; and so he came to attend the Queen Dowager. She had secret relations with him and loved him beyond measure. She became pregnant and, fearing that it would be known, feigned a divination that she should avoid the season, and moved her palace to Yong. Lao Ai was always in attendance, the rewards given him were very rich, and all matters were decided by Lao Ai. Lao Ai's household slaves numbered several thousand, and the guests who sought office by becoming Lao Ai's household retainers more than a thousand.

Biography of Li Si: Li Si was a man of Shangcai in Chu. In his youth he was a petty officer of the Commandery. He saw that the rats in the privy of the officers' quarters ate filth and, being near men and dogs, were constantly startled and frightened by them. Then Si went into the granary and watched the rats there: they ate the stored grain, lived under the great eaves, and had no fear of men or dogs. At this Li Si sighed: "Whether a man is worthy or worthless is like the case of the rats: it lies in where he places himself!"

He then studied the arts of emperors and kings under Xun Qing. When his studies were complete, he judged that the King of Chu was not worth serving and that the Six States were all weak, with no chance of achievement among them, and wished to go west into Qin. Taking leave of Xun Qing he said: "Si has heard that when one meets one's hour one must not be idle. Now the lords of ten thousand chariots are contending for their hour, and it is the travellers who have the management of affairs. Now the King of Qin wishes to swallow all under Heaven and rule under the title of Emperor; this is the hour for commoners to gallop, and the harvest-time of the travelling persuaders. One who sits in a humble and lowly station and makes no plan for himself is a beast staring at meat, with a man's face and able only to walk upright. So there is no greater disgrace than lowliness, no greater sorrow than want. To stay long in a humble station and in straitened circumstances, carping at the age and hating gain, entrusting oneself to inaction: that is not the true feeling of a gentleman. Therefore Si will go west and persuade the King of Qin."

He arrived in Qin just as King Zhuangxiang died. Li Si then sought to become a household retainer of the Chancellor of Qin, Marquis Wenxin Lü Buwei; Buwei thought him able and appointed him a Court Gentleman. Li Si thereby got his chance to speak, and said to the King of Qin: "The petty man is one who lets slip his moment. Those who achieve great deeds do so by seizing on a flaw and being ruthless in following it through. In former days, when Duke Mu of Qin was hegemon, why did he never in the end annex the Six States to the east? Because the Lords were still many and the virtue of Zhou had not yet declined, so the Five Hegemons rose in turn and each in turn honoured the house of Zhou. Since Duke Xiao of Qin, the house of Zhou has sunk low, the Lords have swallowed one another, east of the Pass there are six states, and Qin has ridden its victories and made the Lords its servants for six reigns now. Today the Lords submit to Qin as if they were its Commanderies and Counties. With Qin's strength and the Great King's worth, it would be like sweeping the dust off a stove: enough to wipe out the Lords, complete the imperial task and bring all under Heaven under one rule. This is the one chance in ten thousand generations. If now you are idle and do not hasten to finish it, the Lords will grow strong again and gather to swear the Vertical Alliance, and though you had the worth of the Yellow Emperor you could not annex them." The King of Qin then appointed Si Senior Clerk, followed his plan, and secretly sent out schemers bearing gold and jade to work on the Lords. Those famous men of the Lords who could be brought down with wealth he bound to himself with rich gifts; those who would not, he stabbed with a sharp sword. Having laid his plans to divide rulers from ministers, the King of Qin then sent his good generals in their wake. The King of Qin appointed Si Guest Minister.

It happened that Zheng Guo, a man of Han, came to spy on Qin by building an irrigation canal, and after a time this was discovered. The royal clan and great ministers of Qin all said to the King of Qin: "The men of the Lords who come to serve Qin for the most part only travel here to spy on Qin for their masters; we ask that all guests be expelled without exception." Li Si was counted among those to be expelled. Si then submitted a memorial, saying:

"Your servant has heard that the officers are deliberating the expulsion of the guests; in my humble view this is a mistake. In former days Duke Mu sought gentlemen: in the west he took You Yu from the Rong, in the east he got Baili Xi from Wan, he welcomed Jian Shu from Song, and he brought Pi Bao and Gongsun Zhi from Jin. These five were not born in Qin, yet Duke Mu used them, annexed twenty states and became hegemon over the Western Rong. Duke Xiao used the laws of Shang Yang, changed the ways and altered the customs; the people prospered and multiplied, the state grew rich and strong, the hundred clans were glad to be employed and the Lords submitted in friendship; he captured the armies of Chu and Wei and took a thousand li of land, and to this day the state is well governed and strong. King Hui used the plans of Zhang Yi: he took the lands of Sanchuan, in the west annexed Ba and Shu, in the north gathered in Shang Commandery, in the south took Hanzhong, encompassed the Nine Yi and brought Yan and Ying under control; in the east he seized the fastness of Chenggao and cut off the fat and fertile soil; and so he scattered the Vertical Alliance of the Six States and made them face west and serve Qin, and the benefit of his deeds reaches to this day. King Zhao got Fan Ju, deposed Marquis Rang and expelled Huayang, strengthened the ducal house and barred the private gates, nibbled away at the Lords like a silkworm, and brought Qin to the imperial task. These four lords all owed their success to guests. Seen in this light, how have the guests failed Qin? Had the four lords rejected the guests and not admitted them, kept gentlemen at a distance and not used them, the state would have had none of the substance of wealth and profit, and Qin none of its name for strength and greatness.

"Now Your Majesty obtains the jade of Kunshan, possesses the treasures of Sui and He, hangs up the bright-moon pearl, wears the sword Tai'e, rides the horses of Xianli, raises banners of kingfisher-phoenix plumes and sets up drums of magic alligator hide. Of these several treasures Qin produces not one, yet Your Majesty delights in them: why? If only what the state of Qin produces will do, then the jade disc that shines by night would not adorn the court, vessels of rhinoceros horn and ivory would not be toys and pleasures, the women of Zheng and Wey would not fill the harem, and fine steeds and jueti would not stock the outer stables; the gold and tin of Jiangnan would not be used, nor the cinnabar and azurite of Western Shu for colouring. If what adorns the harem and fills the lower ranks, delighting the heart and pleasing the eye and ear, must come from Qin before it will do, then hairpins of Wan pearls, ear-pendants set with seed-pearls, robes of E gauze and ornaments of brocade and embroidery would not be brought before you, and the lovely, bewitching, graceful women of Zhao, elegant and refined after the fashion, would not stand at your side. Striking pots and beating jars, plucking the zither and slapping the thigh, and howling "wu, wu" to delight the ear: that is the true music of Qin; the music of Zheng, Wey and Sangjian, the Zhao, Yu, Wu and Xiang, are the music of other countries. Now you cast aside the striking of pots and the beating of jars and take up Zheng and Wey, put away the plucking of the zither and take the Zhao and Yu: why so? Because they please you here and now and suit the eye, that is all. But in taking men you do not do so. You ask not whether they will do or not, you weigh not the crooked and the straight; whoever is not of Qin must go, whoever is a guest is expelled. So then what is prized is women, music, pearls and jade, and what is held light is the people. This is not the way to bestride all within the seas and control the Lords.

"Your servant has heard that where the land is broad the grain is plentiful, where the state is great the people are many, and where the arms are strong the soldiers are brave. Thus Taishan does not refuse the clods of earth, and so can achieve its greatness; the rivers and seas do not pick and choose among the little streams, and so can achieve their depth; a true king does not reject the common multitude, and so can make his virtue shine. Thus the land has no four quarters and the people no foreign country; the four seasons are full and fair and the gods and spirits send down blessing: this is why the Five Emperors and the Three Kings had no rival. Now instead you cast off the black-headed people to supply the enemy states, and turn away retainers to build up the Lords, making the gentlemen of all under Heaven draw back and not dare to face west, binding their feet so that they do not enter Qin: this is what is called "lending arms to the bandit and carrying provisions to the thief".

"Things not produced in Qin that may be treasured are many; gentlemen not born in Qin who wish to be loyal are numerous. Now to expel the guests to supply the enemy states, to lose your people to strengthen your foes, emptying yourself within and planting resentment among the Lords without, and then to seek a state free of danger: it cannot be done."

The King of Qin then rescinded the order expelling the guests and restored Li Si to his office, and in the end used his plans. He rose in office to Commandant of Justice. In twenty-odd years Qin at last annexed all under Heaven, honoured its ruler as Emperor, and made Si Chancellor. The Fortresses of the Commanderies and Counties were levelled and their weapons melted down, to show that they would not be used again. Qin was made to have not a foot of land in fief; no sons or brothers were set up as kings, no meritorious ministers as Lords, so that afterwards there should be no trouble of wars and attacks.
